title: How To Strengthen Accountability By Getting Less Involved
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers often unintentionally sabotage their own accountability systems by getting too emotionally and verbally involved when enforcing consequences. He identifies three specific interferences to eliminate: discussing why a student misbehaved (which hands them a ready-made excuse), adding lectures or scolding on top of a consequence (which breeds resentment instead of remorse), and sympathizing with misbehavior because of a student's difficult circumstances (which undermines belief in their capacity to improve). His prescribed alternative is a hands-off approach - letting the stated consequence, such as time-out, stand alone without commentary - so that students feel the full, unmuddied weight of their choices. The piece frames restraint, not additional intervention, as the path to a functioning accountability system.
points: Discussing "why" a student misbehaved often hands them a built-in excuse that undercuts accountability.
Adding lectures or scolding on top of a consequence breeds resentment instead of remorse.
Sympathizing with poor behavior because of a student's home life or struggles signals giving up on them.
A hands-off approach - enforcing the stated consequence and then leaving students alone with it - lets accountability actually work.
quotes: Do you follow your classroom management plan yet still struggle with behavior? Do your students seem unfazed by your accountability measures?

It’s common for teachers to approach students in time-out to talk through why they did what they did. Let me save you the time. Students misbehave because, ultimately, in that particular moment, they wanted to.
The fact is, there is no acceptable reason, excuse, or justification for bad behavior. There is no reason to discuss why.
When you enforce a consequence, resist the urge to add a lecture, a scolding, a sarcastic remark, or anything else that could cause students to resent you.
No matter how difficult home life is for your students, or how tough it is for some to make friends, you do them no favors by sympathizing with their poor behavior.
When you send students to time-out, leave them alone to think. Let them miss being part of the class. Let them feel disappointment in themselves and in their behavior.
Let remorse seep in. Let them stew in their own juices. Let accountability work.
